chapter: New Orleans musicians, recordings and radio
title: Unissued Vocalion sides with King Oliver and Lil, "Don't Pan Me"
summary: Albertson lists three Vocalion sides of late 1926 with Oliver, Lil and possibly Johnny Dodds; she muses about why they were never released and about bootlegging.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: And then you did some recordings
-- three sides that were never issued for Vocalion. You probably did this in Chicago in late '26.
Didn't I do it with my baby sister's name?
with King Oliver and Lil, "Dead Man Blues," "Some Day, Sweetheart" and "Don't Pan Me When I'm Gone." (Sings)
Yeah -- Please don't talk about me when I'm gone --
Is that the same thing as "Don't Pan Me When I'm Gone?"
No -- "Don't Pan Me" -- but they don't use the same words in that one that I have.
But it's the same song, please don't talk about me when I'm gone?
I think they kind of riffed a little bit on it, that song.
Oh, I see.

Other people kind of riffed a little bit on it, stole a little bit from it. See? (Sings) "Don't talk about me -- don't do the things you know are wrong." No, I can't think of it. But anyhow -- that -- but they -- I think they used the same title and did a few different words, but they didn't do the same song that I'm doing there. Uh-huh.
I see. Those things were apparently never issued.
Who did I record them for, Vocallion?
Vocallion with King Oliver and Lil Armstrong.
Is that right.
And possibly Johnny Dodds, it says.
Johnny Dodds.
Yeah, but there seems to be some question as to whether (inaudible) --
Wasn't Johnny playing --
Clarinet --

Clarinet, yes, I remember that. Uh-huh. Yes, I do. I wonder why they didn't put them out, didn't release them. I bet they released them, maybe another name or something like that, another company, and you know how -- those people did a lot of what do you call it, bootlegging.
Bootlegging --
